regions.labelEs: NO ES ALGO QUE SE PUEDA APAGAR.

applications.exampleEs: NO ES ALGO QUE SE PUEDA
applications.explanationEn: No es denies that the thing has the described property, so the ordinary puede changes to the special form pueda after que. Se belongs to the separate passive construction.
The negative description before que calls for pueda instead of the ordinary statement form puede.
Se leaves the person doing the action unnamed, pueda expresses possibility in this description, and apagar stays unchanged.

regions.labelEs: UNA PARTE DE MÍ SIEMPRE ESTÁ SEPARADA.

applications.explanationEn: The -a ending matches parte, which is a feminine singular noun.
Both -yendo forms name simultaneous ongoing mental actions that explain what the detached part is doing.

regions.labelEs: CUANDO DEBERÍAMOS ESTAR MÁS CERCA, PARTE DE MÍ SIGUE SOLO.

applications.explanationEn: Deberíamos gives the “we should” meaning, while estar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Sigue marks a continuing state. The translation uses masculine solo to point semantically to the male speaker; ordinary direct agreement with the feminine noun parte would use sola.

regions.labelEs: CONTANDO LOS ROCES DE SUS DEDOS.

applications.explanationEn: The ongoing-action form contando adds a simultaneous mental action without another conjugated verb.
The owner is the woman in the panel, so sus has the contextual meaning “her.” Its plural form matches the fingers.

regions.labelEs: ROCE. ROCE. ROCE ROCE. ROCE ROCE ROCE. ROCE ROCE ROCE ROCE ROCE.
HICIERA LO QUE HICIERA PARA MERECERTE, NO PUDO HABER SIDO BASTANTE.

applications.explanationEn: Repeating the past subjunctive hiciera around lo que makes every possible past action lead to the same conclusion.
Para introduces the purpose, and the action remains in the unchanged form merecer with te attached.
The object pronoun te attaches directly to the unchanged verb merecer.
Pudo expresses a possibility about the past here, not a successfully completed ability.
Pudo carries the past possibility, while the following helper haber remains unchanged.
Haber stays unchanged, and sido is the completed-action form of ser.

cards.questionEn: Which verb form follows que when you deny that a person or thing exists or has the described property?
cards.answerEn: Use the special subjunctive form after que because the description is being denied, not stated as a fact.
cards.noteEn: An antecedent is the person or thing described by que; a negated antecedent is one the wording presents as absent or not fitting. The special verb form is called the subjunctive. Compare the ordinary statement vive in Conozco a alguien que vive aquí with viva in No conozco a nadie que viva aquí. The plus signs in the prompt mean “followed by.”

example.es: No conozco a nadie que viva aquí.
example.en: I do not know anyone who lives here.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: marks something as receiving a possible action; the doer is not named
cards.noteEn: With a form of poder and an unchanged action verb, se shifts attention away from the person doing the action and toward the thing that can receive it.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action can be done without naming who does it?
cards.answerEn: Use se, then the form of poder that fits the sentence, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: In a direct statement, one thing normally takes puede and several things take pueden. Other sentence types can require forms such as pueda. The final action verb stays unchanged, ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Se keeps the person doing the action unnamed.

cards.answerEn: can (special form used when a possibility is not stated as a fact)
cards.noteEn: Pueda is a special form of poder, the verb meaning “can.” Spanish can use it after que when a description is uncertain, sought, or denied rather than presented as a fact. The ordinary statement form puede changes to pueda.

example.es: Busco a alguien que pueda ayudar.
example.en: I am looking for someone who can help.

cards.answerEn: me (after a preposition such as para)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).
Separada is the feminine singular form of separado. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular person or thing.

example.es: Una pieza está separada del resto.
example.en: One piece is separate from the rest.

cards.answerEn: abstracting; reducing something to its underlying pattern
cards.noteEn: Abstrayendo is the ongoing-action form of abstraer. The spelling changes to yendo in this form, like leyendo from leer.

example.es: Sigue abstrayendo los detalles del problema.
example.en: She keeps abstracting the details of the problem.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.
Viendo is the ongoing-action form of ver. It can mean seeing, watching, or looking at something, depending on context.

example.en: I am looking at the data.

cards.noteEn: Deberíamos is the “we” form of deber used for advice or what ought to happen. The -ríamos ending adds the “would/should” viewpoint: deber becomes deberíamos.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

cards.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of seguir followed by the word that describes the condition.
cards.noteEn: Seguir normally means “to continue” or “to keep going.” Before a description, it means “to still be” or “to remain”: sigue abierta means “is still open.” If the describing word has masculine, feminine, singular, or plural endings, match it to what is being described.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is still in the same condition?

cards.noteEn: When solo describes a masculine person's state, it means alone or lonely rather than “only.” The feminine form is sola.

example.es: Se sintió solo en la ciudad nueva.
example.en: He felt lonely in the new city.

cards.noteEn: Contando is the ongoing-action form of contar, “to count.”
A roce is light contact or a brushing touch. The plural is roces.

example.es: Notó unos roces en la mano.
example.en: He noticed a few light touches on his hand.

cards.noteEn: When context identifies a female owner, sus means “her” before plural things. It agrees with the things owned, not with the owner.

cards.answerEn: the number sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8… in which each later number is the sum of the previous two
cards.noteEn: Starting with 1 and 1, add them to get 2; add 1 and 2 to get 3; then 2 and 3 to get 5. The repeated touches in the comic follow those group sizes, which is why the character recognizes the pattern.
In mathematics, serie can name an ordered sequence of values, although secuencia is also common and is more technically precise in some contexts.

example.es: La serie empieza con uno y uno.
example.en: The sequence begins with one and one.

cards.answerEn: Fibonacci (name associated with a famous number sequence)
cards.noteEn: Fibonacci is the conventional name of the sequence in which each later number is the sum of the two before it.

example.en: We are studying the Fibonacci sequence.

cards.answerEn: I did (special past form used in “whatever I did”)
cards.noteEn: Hiciera is a special past form of hacer, “to do.” This form is called the imperfect subjunctive: it leaves possible past actions open rather than stating one as a fact. Repeating hiciera around lo que creates the reusable pattern hiciera lo que hiciera, “whatever I did.”

example.es: Hiciera lo que hiciera, el resultado era igual.
example.en: Whatever I did, the result was the same.

cards.promptEs: verbo en subjuntivo + lo que + mismo verbo
cards.questionEn: How can you say “whatever someone does” or “whatever happens” when the conclusion stays the same?
cards.answerEn: Use the same special form of the verb before and after lo que.
cards.noteEn: This special form is called the subjunctive. It leaves every possible action open instead of stating one action as a fact. For present time, ordinary hace (“does”) changes to haga: haga lo que haga. In a past setting, hizo or hacía (“did” or “was doing”) can become hiciera: hiciera lo que hiciera. Both repeated forms must match. The plus signs in the prompt mean “followed by.”

example.es: Pase lo que pase, te llamaré.
example.en: Whatever happens, I will call you.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Merecerte combines merecer, “to deserve,” with te, “you.” A short object word such as te can attach to the end of an unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: I hope to deserve you someday.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: could (expressing a possibility about the past)
cards.noteEn: Pudo is a completed-past form of poder for one person or thing. Followed by haber and another completed-action form, it can evaluate what could have happened or been true.

example.en: It could have been a mistake.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

After a verb such as debería, haber remains in its dictionary form and combines with a completed-action form such as llamado or comido. In this construction, haber is a helper rather than the hay construction meaning “there is.”

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to an action that was already completed after another verb such as poder, deber, or parecer?
cards.answerEn: Use the unchanged helper haber followed by the completed-action form of the main verb.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form is often called a participle: terminar becomes terminado, hacer becomes hecho, and ser becomes sido. After another verb, haber stays unchanged. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by.”
Sido is the completed-action form of ser. It follows a form of haber: ha sido means “has been,” and haber sido means “to have been.”
After a verb or adjective, bastante can mean that the amount or degree is sufficient: no es bastante means “it is not enough.”
